title: India Just Raised Cancer Drug Prices by 50 Per Cent. The Iran War Is in Every Chemo Ward Now.
excerpt: Platinum shortages caused by the Gulf conflict have dried up supplies of cisplatin and carboplatin — the first-line drugs for lung, ovarian and bladder cancers. The price hike may restart production, but not everyone will be able to afford it.
body:
India's drug price regulator has raised the ceiling price of two essential chemotherapy drugs by 50 per cent, a decision that reveals just how deeply the Iran war has burrowed into the country's healthcare system.

The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority issued the notification on June 11, hiking the maximum price of cisplatin from ₹7.26 to ₹10.89 per millilitre and carboplatin from ₹60.49 to ₹90.74 per millilitre. The drugs are among the most widely used in oncology — first-line treatments for cancers of the lung, ovaries and bladder — and their shortage has been one of the quieter crises playing out in Indian hospitals over the past two months.

## How Platinum Became a War Casualty

The connection between a Gulf war and a cancer ward in Kolkata is not immediately obvious, but it runs through a single metal: platinum.

Cisplatin and carboplatin are platinum-based compounds. The white metal's price has more than doubled this year, driven by constrained supply from South Africa, rising demand from the automotive industry — which is replacing palladium with platinum in catalytic converters — and dwindling global inventories. The Middle East conflict then piled on, disrupting supply chains and raising manufacturing costs across the board.

Indian generic drugmakers, including Cipla, Intas Pharmaceuticals, Naprod Life Sciences and Venus Remedies, could not absorb the spike. With government price caps locking them into rates set before platinum's surge, several companies temporarily halted production. The result: empty shelves at government hospitals, the very facilities that serve India's poorest cancer patients.

Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai — the country's premier cancer centre — flagged the shortage directly to the pricing authority, lending the crisis an institutional urgency that moved the bureaucracy.

## A One-Time Fix, Not a Cure

The NPPA invoked special provisions of the Drug Price Control Order, used only when public interest demands it. An inter-ministerial committee reviewed 82 applications from pharmaceutical companies seeking price revisions and approved just four — the two platinum-based cancer drugs and two anti-tetanus immunoglobulin injections.

The increase is explicitly framed as a one-time revision, to be reviewed after six months. The regulator acknowledged that "uninterrupted availability" of these drugs is "critical for public health" — a concession that the alternative to higher prices was no drugs at all.

But the arithmetic is sobering. A typical chemotherapy cycle using carboplatin costs between ₹5,000 and ₹15,000 per session at a government hospital. A 50 per cent increase in the drug's ceiling price will not double the bill — the drug is one component among many — but for families already stretching to afford treatment, even a few thousand rupees more per cycle can mean the difference between completing a course and abandoning it.

## The Broader Pattern

The cancer drug crisis is part of a cascading economic toll from the Iran war that India is absorbing across sectors. The government has already extended ₹1.2 trillion in support to oil refiners and retailers to keep fuel prices stable. The fertiliser ministry has sought to double its subsidy allocation. The fiscal deficit is set to widen to 4.8 per cent of GDP, half a percentage point above the February target.

India imports roughly 90 per cent of its platinum, and the metal's price is hostage to the same geopolitical forces that have lifted oil above $85 a barrel and gas by 75 per cent since February. As long as supply chains through the Strait of Hormuz remain disrupted, the knock-on effects will keep reaching places that have nothing to do with tankers or missiles.

## What NRIs Should Know

For the millions of Indians in the diaspora with parents or relatives undergoing cancer treatment back home, the implications are direct. Private hospitals, which price freely above government ceilings, will likely raise rates further. Government hospitals, where these drugs were cheapest, are the ones that ran out first.

The six-month review window means the NPPA will reassess whether prices need to come back down — or go higher. If a ceasefire in the Gulf materialises this weekend, as the White House is suggesting, platinum supply chains could begin to normalise. But metals markets move slowly, and pharmaceutical manufacturing even slower. The reprieve, if it comes, will not arrive in time for the next chemotherapy cycle.
